Minang Malays in Negeri Sembilan, Malaysia 🇲🇾

➖

The name is believed to derive from the nine (sembilan) villages or nagari in the Minangkabau language (now known as luak) settled by the Minang people originally from West Sumatra (in present-day Indonesia). Minangkabau features are still visible today in traditional architecture and the dialect of Malay spoken.

Unlike the hereditary monarchs of the other royal Malay states, the ruler of Negeri Sembilan is known as Yang di-Pertuan Besar instead of Sultan. The election of the Ruler is also unique. He is selected by the council of Undangs who lead the four biggest territories of Sungai Ujong, Jelebu, Johol, and Rembau, making it one of the more democratic monarchies. The Arabic honorific title of the state is Darul Khusus ("the Special Abode") while the form of governance in Negeri Sembilan adopted the Perpatih adat model from its ancestral lands in Minangkabau. This unique form then inspired Malaysia's first Prime Minister, Tunku Abdul Rahman, to implement a constitutional rotational monarchy for the newly independent Malaysian state. Imitating this system, then the position of Yang Agong Pertuan Malaysia was made.

The first king of Malaysia was Tuanku Abdul Rahman from Negeri Sembilan state who is the the fifth descendant of Sultan Abdul Jalil, Pagaruyuang Sultanate, West Sumatra, Indonesia and the following picture is Tuanku Muhriz ibni Almarhum Tuanku Munawir as Sultan as the current Yang di-Pertuan Besar.

The Minangkabaus from Sumatra settled in Negeri Sembilan in the 15th century (the 1400s) under the protection of the Malacca Sultanate, and later under the protection of its successor, the Sultanate of Johor. They also brought their matrilineal custom with them and made it a majority,  and the Linggi River was used as a main trade route since the time of the Malacca Sultanate.

Minang people brought along with them a cultural heritage which is still preserved and practised today as the Adat perpatih, a matrilineal system of inheritance and administration that is unique to the state. It is a system where the husband is the head of the household and inheritance passes from the mother to the daughter. The Minangkabau's divided into twelve suku or tribes, and marriage between members of the same tribe or clan is forbidden. The Minangkabau influence in the state can be found in dances and food as well.

Negeri Sembilan also has traditional music like the Caklempong, Dikir Rebana, Tumbuk Kalang, and Bongai. The musical instruments used bear some semblance to Sumatra, the ancestral home of the Minangkabau people. Dances like the tarian lilin (candle dance) and rentak kuda (beat of the horse) are popular in Negeri Sembilan and the coordinated movements of the dancers in their colorful costumes in the Tarian Piring and the upbeat tempo of Tarian Randai.

Traditional Negeri Sembilan food is hot and spicy, as one of the ingredients used is the chili padi, the hottest of chili peppers. Popular dishes includes rendang, (pieces of beef cooked in coconut milk and chillies).

Text:
TWO THRONES ONE ELECTION
The Crisis That an Election Cannot Solve
Betty Teh | Constituition 

To understand the constitutional crisis that has brought Negeri Sembilan to a simultaneous state election and royal succession dispute, you have to start not on April 19 when four Undang declared the ruler deposed but nearly a year earlier when the seeds of the confrontation were planted. On May 13 2025, Mubarak Dohak, the Undang of Sungai Ujong and the most senior of the four territorial chiefs who hold the power to elect and remove Negeri Sembilan's ruler — was stripped of his title as Datuk Klana Petra following 33 alleged violations of customary and Islamic laws. The decision was made at a meeting of the Telaga Undang, the matriarchal clan leaders and heirs of Sungai Ujong. He was removed not by the ruler. He was removed by his own customary structure.

Mubarak disputed this and refused to vacate. For nearly a year the dispute simmered within Sungai Ujong's customary institutions. Then on April 17 2026, the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang — the council chaired by Tuanku Muhriz held a special session at Istana Besar Seri Menanti. The DKU was presented with the 33 reasons for Mubarak's removal and advised the Luak of Sungai Ujong to formally accept it. Tuanku Muhriz, as chair of the DKU, presided over and accepted that advice. The removal was formalised. Mubarak Dohak was no longer the Undang of Sungai Ujong. Sinar Daily

Two days later Mubarak struck back.

On April 19, Mubarak appeared at the Balai Undang Luak Sungai Ujong alongside three other Undang — Maarof Mat Rashad of Jelebu, Muhammed Abdullah of Johol and Abdul Rahim Yasin of Rembau and read a declaration deposing Tuanku Muhriz as Yang di Pertuan Besar. No specific reasons were given. No full enquiry had been conducted. The declaration was announced at a press conference and streamed on Facebook. 

The same man whose removal had just been formalised by the DKU two days earlier was now using his claimed authority as Undang to depose the ruler who had just accepted that removal. 

The state government rejected the declaration immediately. Aminuddin declared it void on the most basic of grounds — Mubarak had been removed from office with effect from May 13 2025 and had no authority to sign or read any declaration as Undang. 

But the other three Undang disputed this entirely. They issued a statement saying the DKU on April 17 had not made a collective and unanimous decision on Mubarak's removal, calling Aminuddin's account untrue and not in accordance with the Negeri Sembilan constitution. They also declared that Aminuddin was no longer fit to lead the state administration and should be replaced. 

Two versions of what happened in the same DKU meeting on April 17. The government's version — Mubarak was validly removed. The Undang's version — no such unanimous decision was made. The minutes of that meeting became so contested that the three Undang and Mubarak filed an originating summons in the Seremban High Court seeking a copy of the DKU meeting minutes. 

This is the origin of everything that followed. Not a sudden eruption after 18 years of stable rule. A confrontation that had been building since May 2025 when Mubarak lost his title within his own customary structure and which detonated on April 19 when he chose the most dramatic available instrument of retaliation: the constitutional power to depose a ruler.

To understand why that power exists and why it created such a crisis when invoked, you have to understand what makes Negeri Sembilan constitutionally unique. Every other Malay state has a hereditary monarchy — the throne passes from father to son, predetermined by bloodline. Negeri Sembilan has never done this. Under the Adat Perpatih system, a matrilineal customary law tradition established in 1773 and derived from the Minangkabau people of West Sumatra — the Yang di Pertuan Besar is elected by four territorial chiefs known as the Undang Yang Empat. The Undang of Sungai Ujong, Rembau, Jelebu and Johol collectively hold the power to install the ruler. 

Under Article 10 of the written Negeri Sembilan state constitution which codified the adat — they also hold the power to remove him under four specified conditions: insanity, stupidity, acts that disgrace Islam, or acts that disgrace the royal institution. But crucially the constitution requires a full and complete enquiry before any such removal. No enquiry was held on April 19. The declaration was made without one.

The legal problem with the April 19 declaration therefore has two independent bases. Former judge Hishamudin said it was invalid first because Mubarak who signed and read it had already been removed as Undang and had no authority to act. And second because no full enquiry had been conducted as required by Article X of the state constitution. Either ground alone was sufficient to make the declaration void. Together they made it constitutionally indefensible. 

Yet the three remaining Undang stood by it. And they had their own legal strategist in the form of Tan Sri Rais Yatim, former law minister, Negeri Sembilan native, and the public voice of the traditionalist faction — who argued that all adat procedures had been properly followed. 

Two lawyers. Two readings of the same constitutional text. Both citing the same articles. Neither willing to concede.

The crisis did not stay within the palace. Four days after the April 19 declaration, the Negeri Sembilan State Legislative Assembly was scheduled to open its first meeting of the fourth session, a routine constitutionally required sitting that must occur at least once every six months. The Undang issued a statement the night before demanding postponement until all customary transfer of power processes were completed. Tuanku Muhriz arrived anyway. His arrival at Wisma Negeri on April 23 accompanied by his consort, his inspection of the guard of honour, and his delivery of the royal address was the first time in his entire reign since 2008 that the four Undang had not attended a state assembly opening. 

All 36 assemblymen were present except one on official duty. The Speaker adjourned the sitting immediately after the royal address, saying he hoped the dispute could be clarified before the next sitting. The assembly opened and adjourned on the same day. 

The royal crisis then consumed the political one. Fourteen UMNO state assemblymen withdrew their support from Menteri Besar Aminuddin citing his perceived alignment with Tuanku Muhriz against the Undang. PH fell to seventeen seats in a thirty six seat assembly, two short of a majority. 

The government that had defended the constitution's position on the ruler's legitimacy was now itself rendered constitutionally uncertain. The two crises fed each other. Aminuddin's defence of Tuanku Muhriz's legitimacy became the grounds for his own government's delegitimisation. The UMNO assemblymen who chose the Undang over the constitution had effectively handed the traditionalist faction a second instrument of pressure — the assembly numbers.

Then June 5 produced its extraordinary scenes. On the same day Aminuddin dissolved the assembly with Tuanku Muhriz's consent, police blocked the Undang from entering the venue for their planned DKU meeting in Tampin. The High Court issued an interim injunction halting proceedings. The Undang relocated to a hotel in Alor Gajah in Melaka, a different state entirely and there proclaimed Tunku Nadzaruddin as Yang di Pertuan Besar for the second time. 

Anwar reaffirmed Tuanku Muhriz as the legitimate ruler and questioned the dignity of a royal proclamation conducted in a hotel. 

Two men now claim the throne. One recognised by the federal government, the state government, and the courts. One recognised by the four chiefs who have held the constitutional power to elect rulers since 1773. 

And an election has been called to resolve a political crisis that the dissolution itself cannot resolve — because the deeper constitutional question of who is the legitimate Yang di Pertuan Besar will outlast any electoral result.

If PH wins and Aminuddin returns as MB he will continue recognising Tuanku Muhriz. If BN wins a new MB must decide before whom he takes his oath. Which ruler signs the instruments of government. Which ruler's consent is required for future dissolutions. The election produces a government. It does not produce an answer.

What makes this crisis genuinely unprecedented is not its complexity but its location. It lives in the gap between two legal systems that have coexisted in Negeri Sembilan for 253 years — the written constitution and the unwritten adat. The written constitution codified the adat but did not resolve what happens when they contradict each other. 

For 253 years that contradiction never fully surfaced. It surfaced on May 13 2025 when Mubarak Dohak lost his title. It detonated on April 19 2026 when he used the most powerful instrument available to him to strike back. And it has not been resolved by courts, injunctions, proclamations in hotel ballrooms, or the dissolution of a state assembly. 

Sixty days of campaigning will not resolve it either.
Another layer to the N9 palace intrigue.

Text:
Malaysia’s Conference of Rulers postponed over NS ruler’s legitimacy

Issue now potentially could undermine the stability of the monarchy

As the prime minister Anwar Ibrahim calls on royalty to be left out of politics, there is some community concerns over a number of Royal decrees, and the DAP’s Tony Pua has raised questions about royal roles in politics and the role of the Sedition Act.
It is now during this time that the Conference of Rulers has been postponed at short notice amid an ongoing dispute over the throne of Negeri Sembilan, underscoring the paramount importance of preserving the stability and unity of the constitutional monarchy.
The rare cancellation of the meeting, originally scheduled for June 23 to 25, reflects the deep concern among the nine rulers over the unfolding crisis in Negeri Sembilan. Such postponements are highly uncommon. The last occurring during the Covid-19 lockdowns in 2021. This highlights how seriously the institution views any threat to the established order and harmony within the royal houses.
At the heart of the matter are competing claims to the position of Yang di-Pertuan Besar. The state and federal governments continue to recognise Tuanku Muhriz Munawir as the rightful ruler. However, the four Undang (territorial chieftains) have moved to install his nephew, Tunku Nadzaruddin Ja’afar, prompting a complex legal and customary dispute. This uncertainty has already triggered the dissolution of the state legislative assembly on June 5, raising questions about the feasibility and appropriateness of proceeding with state elections on August 1.
The Conference of Rulers serves as a vital pillar of Malaysia’s constitutional framework, providing a forum for the monarchs to deliberate on matters of national importance, including those affecting Malay customs, Islam, and constitutional amendments. Any perception of division or unresolved conflict within this esteemed body risks eroding public confidence in the monarchy’s stabilizing role. In a diverse nation like Malaysia, the monarchy’s continuity and impartial dignity are essential safeguards for national unity and social harmony.
Background rooted in Adat Perpatih
Under Negeri Sembilan’s unique Adat Perpatih customs, the Undang hold traditional authority to elect and, in exceptional cases following due inquiry, remove a ruler. Tensions reportedly escalated after disagreements over privileges and a decision by Tuanku Muhriz regarding the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang (DKU). The subsequent sequence of events, including the Undang’s removal ceremony on April 19, the state government’s late-night announcement of dissolution, and the attempted installation of the new claimant have all created a delicate situation now before the courts.
Interim court injunctions have been issued, and the matter is slated for further hearings in July. Both sides have acted within what they view as their legitimate roles, yet the priority must now be a clear, orderly, and legally sound resolution that upholds the dignity of the institution and respects established conventions. Prolonged uncertainty serves no one and could inadvertently politicize an institution that should remain above partisan contention.
Broader implications for stability
The dispute has already had political repercussions, including shifts in support within the state assembly and implications for Pakatan Harapan (PH) ahead of the polls. A further erosion of institutional clarity could complicate governance and public trust at a time when political stability is already under pressure from other state elections, such as the upcoming one in Johor.
Malaysia’s monarchy has long been a symbol of continuity and a moderating force in the nation’s federal democracy. The rulers’ decision to pause the conference demonstrates prudent leadership and a collective commitment to safeguarding the monarchy’s integrity rather than allowing rushed proceedings that might deepen divisions. A swift and amicable resolution, ideally through dialogue, respect for custom, and judicial clarity is in the best interest of Negeri Sembilan and the federation as a whole.
The next scheduled Conference of Rulers in October will offer an important opportunity to reaffirm unity. In the interim, all parties are urged to exercise restraint, prioritize legal channels, and place the long-term stability and reverence of the royal institution above all other considerations. The strength of Malaysia’s constitutional monarchy lies in its enduring role as a unifying pillar, a role that must be protected with care.

Why? Because one wrong move by the Monarchs, and the entire definition of a Constitutional Monarchy will collapse.

Text:
THE THRONE, THE UNDANG, AND THE DAY ADAT STARTED ARGUING WITH ITSELF

There are few things Malaysians assume will remain stable forever.

The sunrise.

The price of nasi lemak eventually going up.

Traffic jams appearing from nowhere.

And royal succession.

The first three occasionally surprise us.

The fourth is not supposed to.

Which is why the recent turmoil surrounding Negeri Sembilan has left many Malaysians staring at their phones the way one stares at a GPS that suddenly announces:

“Please drive into the lake.”

Because for a brief moment, it seemed as though an ancient institution built on centuries of custom had wandered into a constitutional maze while carrying several competing maps.

And nobody appeared entirely certain which map was the official one.

⸻

THE STATE WHERE DEMOCRACY’S OLDER COUSIN STILL LIVES

Most Malaysians understand monarchy through a simple formula.

King dies.

Prince succeeds.

People shout “Daulat Tuanku.”

Lunch is served.

Negeri Sembilan, however, has always been the intellectual in the family.

The cousin who insists on explaining the rules before playing the game.

Its royal system is not built upon simple inheritance.

It is built upon Adat Perpatih.

Consensus.

Selection.

Customary authority.

Institutional layers.

Historical legitimacy.

In other words, Negeri Sembilan’s political architecture resembles a beautifully handcrafted antique clock.

Elegant.

Unique.

Sophisticated.

And occasionally so complicated that nobody remembers which gear moves which hand.

⸻

WHEN EVERYONE CLAIMS TO BE THE REAL REFEREE

The problem with legitimacy is that it functions much like Wi-Fi.

Nobody notices it when it works.

Everybody notices it when it doesn’t.

In ordinary times, the authority of an Undang appears settled.

The authority of the Yang di-Pertuan Besar appears settled.

The authority of customary institutions appears settled.

Then suddenly competing groups emerge.

Each side cites custom.

Each side cites law.

Each side cites history.

Each side cites procedure.

Each side insists it is defending tradition.

And the ordinary rakyat begins feeling like a spectator watching two lawyers argue over ownership of the same house while the house itself is still occupied.

The result is not clarity.

The result is confusion wearing ceremonial attire.

⸻

ADAT: THE WORLD’S OLDEST OPERATING SYSTEM

There is a curious habit among Malaysians.

Whenever custom is discussed, people split into two tribes.

The first tribe treats adat as sacred software.

Never update.

Never modify.

Never question.

The second tribe treats adat as an old Nokia phone.

Interesting historically.

Not especially useful today.

Both positions miss something important.

Custom survives because it adapts.

Otherwise every civilisation would still be travelling by buffalo cart and communicating through smoke signals.

The irony is that traditions which survive centuries are usually the traditions most capable of evolving.

The traditions that refuse all adaptation eventually become museum exhibits.

Beautiful.

Respected.

And largely irrelevant to daily life.

⸻

THE RESORT, THE PROCLAMATION, AND THE NATIONAL DOUBLE TAKE

Politics occasionally produces strange optics.

This episode produced extraordinary optics.

A proclamation.

A royal dispute.

A competing narrative.

And a location that generated almost as much discussion as the proclamation itself.

The entire affair felt less like a carefully choreographed constitutional process and more like a historical drama whose script had accidentally escaped into social media before the final edit.

For ordinary Malaysians unfamiliar with Negeri Sembilan’s constitutional intricacies, the spectacle raised obvious questions.

If a proclamation can be made publicly, who has authority?

If authority is disputed, who decides?

If everyone claims legitimacy, where does legitimacy actually reside?

These are not merely legal questions.

They are existential questions for any institution.

⸻

WHEN CUSTOM MEETS FACEBOOK

In previous centuries, customary disputes remained largely within customary circles.

Village leaders discussed them.

Traditional authorities resolved them.

The wider public heard about them months later, if at all.

Today?

A disagreement can become a livestream.

A proclamation can become a TikTok clip.

A constitutional argument can become a WhatsApp forward before breakfast.

Custom moves at the speed of tradition.

Social media moves at the speed of caffeine.

The collision is inevitable.

And institutions built for patience suddenly find themselves being judged by audiences demanding answers before lunchtime.

⸻

“BIAR MATI ANAK, JANGAN MATI ADAT” — REALLY?

Perhaps the most fascinating aspect of the debate is how often Malaysians invoke the famous proverb:

“Biar mati anak, jangan mati adat.”

People quote it with such confidence one might assume they have personally tested the policy.

Let us be honest.

Nobody chooses tradition over their child.

Nobody.

Not the loudest defender of custom.

Not the fiercest guardian of heritage.

Not the uncle giving lectures at weddings.

The proverb was never meant to be taken literally.

It was meant to emphasise the importance of social order.

But somewhere along the way, some people began treating it as though customs exist for their own sake rather than for the wellbeing of the community they are supposed to serve.

That is like preserving the steering wheel while forgetting the purpose of the car.

⸻

THE REAL CRISIS IS NOT THE THRONE

The deepest issue may not be who occupies the throne.

Nor who signs which proclamation.

Nor which faction claims legitimacy.

The deeper issue is public confidence.

Institutions survive not only through legal authority.

They survive through belief.

The moment ordinary people begin asking:

“Who is actually in charge?”

an institution has entered dangerous territory.

Because authority depends on recognition.

And recognition depends on trust.

⸻

CONCLUSION: WHEN THE ROOTS ARGUE, THE TREE SHAKES

Negeri Sembilan’s unique system has survived wars, colonialism, independence, modernisation, and globalisation.

That alone deserves respect.

But every living institution eventually encounters the same challenge.

How does it preserve tradition while maintaining legitimacy in a modern world?

How does it honour history without becoming trapped by it?

How does it ensure that custom remains a source of stability rather than confusion?

Because ultimately, the strength of a throne does not come from wood, gold, titles, or ceremonies.

It comes from confidence.

And confidence, unlike custom, cannot be inherited.

It must be renewed.

Again and again.

Wallahua’lam.

When branches argue, leaves tremble.

But when roots argue, the entire tree begins to wonder where it stands.

KUALA LUMPUR, April 30 — Datuk Mubarak Dohak has been ordered to immediately vacate the official residence at Balai Luak Undang Sungei Ujong, where he has stayed for more than three decades.

A notice dated April 29 issued by the Negeri Sembilan State Secretary’s Office (SUK) began circulating on Thursday, according a report published by Sinar Harian today.

The letter, signed by Management Services Division secretary Akmal Farid Rizal Noordin, stated that the directive follows a Special Sitting of the Council of Justice and Custom (Dewan Keadilan dan Undang, DKU) held on April 17.

“In view of this, you are instructed to vacate the official residence and Balai Undang Luak Sungei Ujong with immediate effect. All state government assets registered at the premises must be kept in good condition for future inspection,” it said.

However, state secretary Datuk Mohd Zafir Ibrahim declined to confirm the eviction order when contacted.

Sources said state staff serving at the premises have also been instructed to be reassigned.

A check at the location showed no sign of eviction activity, and Mubarak is understood to still be residing there.

Previously, Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Aminuddin Harun said Mubarak’s actions in signing and reading out a declaration purportedly removing the Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, could not be recognised.

He said Mubarak no longer had authority or function as Undang Luak Sungei Ujong, adding that the move was not in line with Articles 10 to 12 of the Negeri Sembilan Constitution.

The dispute over the Sungei Ujong adat institution surfaced after Waris Luak Sungei Ujong issued a statement on March 18 announcing Mubarak’s removal as Datuk Klana Petra Undang Luak Sungei Ujong, alleging breaches of religious and customary law.

The statement was issued by Tua Lembaga Waris di-Darat, Datuk Andulika Mandalika Zainol Ariffin Ibrahim, following consent from senior customary representatives.

However, the Sungei Ujong Adat Lembaga Datuk-Datuk later issued a counter statement on April 18 declaring unanimous support for Mubarak.

It said the March 18 declaration was invalid under adat rules, as Zainol Ariffin had already been removed from his position in November 2024.

The group stressed that any appointment or removal of an Undang must follow customary procedures in line with the Negeri Sembilan Constitution (1959), Clause 14 (1) and (3).

It also urged external parties not to interfere in Sungei Ujong adat affairs.

“I am informed that the selection of the 22nd Undang of Rembau was conducted in accordance with the adat (customs) and traditions practised in Rembau.

For matters relating to the ceremony and preparations, the adat leaders may discuss them with the Orang Empat Istana. I pray that all arrangements proceed smoothly,” he said.

Meanwhile, chairman of the Kerapatan Buapak Delapan ceremony for the Biduanda Nan Dua Carak customary clan, Datuk Juan Datuk Zulkipli Shamsudin, said Hassan Ab Hamid, 67, had been selected as the 22nd Undang of Rembau in accordance with established adat procedures.

Zulkipli stressed that under the Adat Perpatih system, an Undang is not appointed by the Yang Dipertuan Besar but is chosen through the customary processes of the luak itself.

“The role of His Royal Highness is to receive representatives of the luak when they seek an audience and, when required by custom, to grant consent and recognition to the decision reached by the community.

“His Royal Highness does not summon, choose or appoint any individual at his own discretion. Any statement suggesting otherwise reflects a misunderstanding of the adat that have governed Negeri Sembilan for centuries,” he said.

PETALING JAYA: The Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, today said that the state’s administration must continue to function as usual to ensure orderly governance and safeguard the interests of the people.

Tuanku Muhriz said the absence of the state dignitaries who usually accompany him at the opening of state assembly sessions – the four Undangs (chieftains) and the Tunku Besar of Tampin – did not affect the legitimacy of the proceedings.

“I pray to Allah that my state and its people will continue to be blessed with prosperity and harmony under the leadership of menteri besar Aminuddin Harun and the state executive council,” he said.

“I am deeply grateful that the strong cooperation within my government has continued to deliver excellent performance over the past year,” he said in his royal address at the opening ceremony of the fourth session of the 15th Negeri Sembilan state legislative assembly at Wisma Negeri, Seremban.

The Tunku Ampuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Aishah Rohani Tengku Besar Mahmud, was also in attendance.

On Monday, Aminuddin said the state government did not recognise the recent move to depose Tuanku Muhriz as the Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan.

The former Undang of Sungai Ujong, Mubarak Dohak, announced the removal of Tuanku Muhriz in a press conference with the three other Undangs last Sunday.

In Negeri Sembilan, the four Undangs represent the main traditional districts or luak: Sungai Ujong, Jelebu, Johol, and Rembau.

The four Undangs are traditional territorial chiefs who play a central role in electing the Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan and advising on customary law under the state’s adat perpatih.

森美兰当前的政治与制度冲突，与其说是数字上的危机，不如说是一场宪政成熟度的考验。该州以“习俗法”（adat）为基础的独特治理体系，由最高元首端姑严端大臣（Tuanku Yang di-Pertuan Besar）与四大酋长（Undang Yang Empat）为核心，如今正与巫统内部派系运作、昌明团结政府（MADANI）的政策再校准，以及国盟（Perikatan Nasional）的策略性调整交织在一起。关键问题不在于谁声称拥有合法性，而在于当合法性对政治便利构成约束时，谁仍然选择尊重它。

问题的核心，体现出一种熟悉的模式：巫统内部派系试图在一个强调纪律的联盟架构中重新调整影响力。州务大臣的地位，从宪法角度出发，并在森美兰制度中获得强化，原则上应免受周期性派系压力的干扰。然而，当前发展却显示并非如此。正在发生的，并非法律真空，而是将政治竞争叠加在一个原本旨在防止不稳定的制度之上。

因此，“谁”并不模糊。这涉及巫统内部的竞争派系、扎希哈米迪阵营的领导考量、安华依布拉欣政府整体的稳定导向，以及最高元首在四大酋长协商下所行使的制度权威。“什么”同样清晰：这是一种试图以或明或暗的方式影响政治结果的行为，其本质是在测试宪政规范的边界。

时间点同样具有启示意义。这种摩擦出现在选举前的政治环境中，各方正重新定位、巩固影响力，并测试制度极限。这类时刻往往揭示，治理框架究竟是约束政治行为的护栏，还是仅具形式意义的结构。森美兰的制度设计——结合宪法与习俗权威——本应发挥前者的功能。如今，政治行为者是否尊重这一设计，正受到检验。

从治理角度看，州务大臣的合法性并非源自派系背书，而是源自宪政程序。最高元首与四大酋长的参与，为制度提供了一层本应足以缓冲政治波动的监督机制。当派系试图重新诠释或挑战这一结构时，问题已不再是政治分歧，而是制度纪律本身。

在这一点上，安华依布拉欣与扎希哈米迪之间的差异，具有分析意义。根据可观察的政策立场，安华依布拉欣更倾向于制度连续性与联盟稳定。昌明框架依赖可预测性，无法承受由内部派系调整所引发的反复波动。相较之下，扎希哈米迪必须面对巫统内部压力，而这些压力往往将党内整合置于联盟平衡之上。这种张力未必是直接对抗，但却是结构性存在：一方在管理国家联盟，另一方在管理内部仍存分歧的政党。

国盟的立场，则为局势增添另一层复杂性。其定位似乎较少基于宪政一致性，而更多依赖政治机会。当治理框架受到尊重时，反对党应以政策替代方案作为批评重点；当同一框架被选择性挑战时，相关叙事便更接近策略性操作。这种不一致性难以忽视：制度合法性在有利时被维护，在不利时则受到质疑。

因此，这场冲突的“如何发生”，与其“为何发生”同样重要。政治行为者并未公开拆解制度结构，而是在测试其弹性。他们通过叙事建构、选择性诠释宪政规范，以及放大派系不满来实现这一点。这是一种常见策略，但未必具有可持续性。一旦制度被视为可协商对象，其稳定功能便会削弱。

从经济角度看，其影响并非抽象。治理公信力直接影响投资者信心，尤其是在森美兰这样一个政治稳定与发展规划高度关联的州属。投资者更关注制度可预测性，而非单纯的政治竞争。当治理表现被视为取决于派系动态时，风险溢价将随之上升。

更广泛的启示其实相当直接。宪政体系并非自我执行，它依赖政治行为者对法律精神与条文的共同尊重。森美兰融合习俗与宪法权威的制度，本身具备稳固结构。当前紧张局势，并非制度失败，而是制度内政治纪律的考验。

展望未来，数项务实步骤至关重要。首先，各方必须重申最高元首与四大酋长在州体制中的最终仲裁角色。其次，巫统领导层需通过制度化机制解决内部派系问题，而非将其外溢为治理争议。第三，昌明政府必须维持一致立场，将制度连续性置于短期政治妥协之上。最后，反对阵营若要被视为具备替代能力，其批评亦须建立在宪政一致性之上。

森美兰的局势，最终反映出一个更广泛的国家现实：政治公信力，已不再由主张决定，而是由对制度秩序的遵守来衡量。稳定并非口头宣示，而是通过纪律体现。那些将宪政框架视为可灵活操作工具者，最终可能发现，无论是市场、选民还是制度本身，所展现的容忍度远低于预期。

The “what” is equally clear: an attempt, subtle or otherwise, to influence political outcomes in ways that test the boundaries of constitutional propriety.

Timing, as always, is instructive. The friction emerges in a pre-election environment where political actors are recalibrating positions, consolidating influence, and testing institutional limits. Such moments often reveal whether governance frameworks function as guardrails or mere formalities. Negeri Sembilan’s system, with its layered constitutional and customary authority, is designed to act as the former. Whether political actors respect that design is now under scrutiny.

From a governance perspective, the Menteri Besar’s legitimacy is not derived from factional endorsement but from constitutional process. The involvement of the Tuanku Yang di-Pertuan Besar and the Undang Yang Empat introduces a level of institutional oversight that should, in theory, neutralise political volatility. When factions attempt to reinterpret or challenge that structure, the issue is no longer political disagreement but institutional discipline.

The MADANI framework depends on predictability; it cannot afford episodic disruptions driven by internal factional recalibration. Zahid Hamidi, on the other hand, must navigate internal UMNO pressures that often prioritise party consolidation over coalition equilibrium. The tension is not necessarily confrontational, but it is structurally embedded. One side is managing a national coalition; the other is managing a party with unresolved internal alignments.

Perikatan Nasional’s stance adds another layer of complexity. Its positioning appears less anchored in constitutional consistency and more in political opportunity. When governance frameworks are respected, opposition critique should focus on policy alternatives. When the same frameworks are selectively challenged, the narrative begins to resemble tactical opportunism. The inconsistency is difficult to ignore: institutional legitimacy is defended when advantageous and questioned when inconvenient.

The “how” of this conflict is therefore as important as the “why.” Political actors are not openly dismantling institutional structures; they are testing their elasticity. It is a familiar strategy, though not necessarily a sustainable one. Institutions, once perceived as negotiable, lose their stabilising function.

From an economic perspective, the implications are not abstract. Governance credibility directly influences investor confidence, particularly in a state like Negeri Sembilan where political stability is intertwined with development planning. Investors are less concerned with political competition than with institutional predictability. When governance appears contingent on factional dynamics, risk premia adjust accordingly.

The broader lesson is straightforward. Constitutional systems are not self-enforcing; they rely on political actors to respect both the letter and the spirit of the law. Negeri Sembilan’s framework, with its integration of adat and constitutional authority, provides a robust structure. The current tension is therefore not a failure of the system, but a test of political discipline within it.

Second, UMNO leadership must address internal factionalism through structured mechanisms rather than externalising it into governance disputes. Third, the MADANI administration must maintain a consistent stance that prioritises institutional continuity over short-term political accommodation. Finally, opposition actors must align critique with constitutional consistency if they are to be regarded as credible alternatives.

Negeri Sembilan’s situation ultimately illustrates a broader national truth: political credibility is no longer determined by assertion, but by adherence to institutional order. Stability is not merely declared; it is demonstrated through discipline. Those who treat constitutional frameworks as flexible instruments may find that markets, voters, and institutions themselves are far less accommodating.

He claims that the position was reached after he held discussions with the assemblymen today following their move to withdraw support for Negeri Sembilan menteri besar Aminuddin Harun.

So is the crisis over? 

I seriously doubt it. 

For one, the 14 Umno aduns have yet to withdraw their withdrawal of support of Aminuddin's government, nor have they reasserted their support for his continuous rule.

So in my view, Zahid Hamidi's claim, even if true, does not mean that the crisis in Negeri Sembilan has been resolved - rather, it likely just indicates that the there is a truce between Umno-PN and the PH in Negeri Sembilan for the time eing, and the truce that they have forged is likely of the sort that Donald Trump has forged with Iran - it is a truce that is destined to be broken, and that too in the very near future. 

In my personal opinion, Umno Negeri Sembilan is likely just waiting to see how the feud between the Tuanku Muhriz and the 4 Undangs will play out, before they decide their next move. 

Regardless of whether it is Tuanku Muhriz or the 4 undangs that will come out on top, Umno will then continue to press on with its claim for the N9 state government, because why wouldn't it? 

Together with PN, who has declared support for it, it has the majority of the seat in the state assembly. 

Cooperation with PN is also the only way that Umno Negeri Sembilan will be able to seize Negeri Sembilan back from PH. 

Considering that, it is extremely unlikely that Umno Negeri Sembilan will let this golden opportunity slip away, regardless of what Zahid Hamidi claims.

To reinforce Tuanku Muhriz's position as the King of Negeri Sembilan, Aminuddin's government has also recently ordered for the official residence of the Sungai Ujong undang and the Balai Undang of Luak Sungai Ujong to be vacated.

In a letter issued to the private secretary of Mubarak Dohak, the former undang of Sungai Ujong, a division secretary from the Negeri Sembilan state secretary’s office wrote:

“You are hereby instructed to vacate the official residence and the Balai Undang of Luak Sungai Ujong with immediate effect.” 

The move by Aminuddin's government is likely made to weaken the position of the Undangs and strengthen the position of Tuanku Muhriz. 

But considering that there has been no replacement to Mubarak Dohak, and that the other Undangs are still unanimously standing with Mubarak, the position of Tuanku Muhriz is still on shaky grounds, because the condition for him to rule  - which is the support of the 4 undangs - are still absent. 

Unless this issue is fixed, even if Aminuddin's government removes all the Undangs from their official residence, the royal crisis in Negeri Sembilan cannot be considered as resolved. 

While the crisis in Negeri Sembilan continues to unfold, unfortunately, the media, instead of being a neutral and objective reporter of the unfolding events, has decided to join the fray and put its thumb on the scale. 

A lot of people, especially the media, like to talk about "institutional and structural reforms" in Malaysia - but like many people in our country,  just because they say the word, it doesn't mean they know what it means. 

You see, our institutions are like a house or a building - they are structures - and like any structure, they have to fulfill certain conditions in order to stand, or else they will collapse or become dysfunctional. 

For a building of a certain size, for example, you must have a certain amount of pillars and its foundation has to be a certain measure deep and there is a limit to how much you can modify and shape it. 

Just because you have the money or power, you can't make a building any which way you please - you must make it in accordance to its design and within the limits of its parameters, or it won't be able to stand in reality. 

It is the same with our country's institution - we can't just do whatever we want with our instititutions just because we have the power, wealth, influence or position - if we do, the entire structure will collapse. 

It is because people with power, position, influence and wealth have been doing whatever they want with our institutions, just to satisfy their short term interest and goals, that for decades, we have been calling for institutional and structural reforms.  

Unfortunately, the media, which we had always assumed was a champion for structural and institutional reform, is now showing its true colours, by acting like just another entity that believes that it can do whatever it wants with our institutions, simply because it has the influence to do so.  

They are doing it by openly siding in favour of one side over the other, in the political crisis in Negeri Sembilan. 

Just a couple of days ago, at least one media organisation has blatantly declared that "voters in Negeri Sembilan do not want a snap election to break the deadlock in Negeri Sembilan", without any basis. It seems that that the said media outlet had just called a few people in Negeri Sembilan to ask for their opinions, and based on this extremely flimsy grounds, it then brazenly declared that snap elections should not be held in Negeri Sembilan, by presumptuously usurping the voice of the people. 

If you are thinking "c'mon Nehru, you can't just condemn the media based on that one incident - one swallow doesn't make a summer, " well guess what, it is not just one swallow. 

Just a few days ago, the media also reported that the former New Straits Times chief editor Kalimullah Hassan has opined that the fact that hundreds of congregants at Masjid Negeri Negeri Sembilan in Seremban, who would normally disperse after prayers, lined up to greet the ruler, show that the public support the Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir.

There is actually no reason for the media to even platform Kalimullah's view, when Kalimullah is probably just a retiree, other than to manufacture public opinion. 

Today, it is also reporting that 12 organisations has gathered to show its support for the Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, at a mosque in Jempol, likely to perpetuate the narrative that it is the will of the people that Tuanku Muhriz continues to reign. 

That the media is usurping the "people's will", likely to advocate for the side that it favours, is at best, an indication that even the media is ignorant of  what terms like "structural reforms" or "institutional reforms"actually means, or at worse, an indication that the media is no different from other entities in the country - which it itself has for decades rallied against-  for eroding the institutional structure in the country, in order forward its personal agendas. 

If you respect our institutions and the structure that maintains it, you will respect the conditions that uphold it. 

In the way that our primary institutions is structured, it is only the legislative branch that requires the "people's mandate" as a condition to exist and  function. 

Other institutions, like the Judiciary and the Royalty, do not require the "people's mandate" to exist and function. 

Institutions like the royalty and judiciary,  have their own conditions to fulfill, which does not include popular mandate, in order to exist and function. 

In the case of the Negeri Sembilan throne, for example, they have their own institutionalized traditions and customs, to determine who is to serve as their king.

In their traditions and customs, the ruler of Negeri Sembilan rules with the support of the Negeri Sembilan chieftains, or Undangs, and not by popular mandate. 

That the media is trying to distort the institutional structure of Negeri Sembilan, by indicating that popular support is a determinant of who gets to rule Negeri SEmbilan,  likely to forward its own agenda and support its own biases, is thus deeply regretful. 

Now you might be thinking that I am just saying what I am saying because I champion the interest of Umno Negeri Sembilan or the Undangs, but to that, I will just say that it is precisely that mentality that has caused  a deep rot to set into the structure of our institutions.

If you wish to reform our institutions at a structural level, change your mentality. 

Instead of determining who you support first, and then bending our institutions, even at structural level, to ensure that you or those you support win, you must instead keep your faith in the customs, traditions and practices of our institutions, even if it causes you or those who you favour to lose. 

If you cannot do that, then even if you shout "institutional reform, institutional reform,institutional reform" for a thousand years, nothing is going to change.

🗓️ April 28, 2026 | 森美兰权力与原则的考验：当宪政秩序遇上政治野心
𝙲𝚑𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚜𝚎 𝚅𝚎𝚛𝚜𝚒𝚘𝚗 𝙲𝚘𝚖𝚖𝚎𝚗𝚝𝚊𝚛𝚢

森美兰当前的政治与制度冲突，与其说是数字上的危机，不如说是一场宪政成熟度的考验。该州以“习俗法”（adat）为基础的独特治理体系，由最高元首端姑严端大臣（Tuanku Yang di-Pertuan Besar）与四大酋长（Undang Yang Empat）为核心，如今正与巫统内部派系运作、昌明团结政府（MADANI）的政策再校准，以及国盟（Perikatan Nasional）的策略性调整交织在一起。关键问题不在于谁声称拥有合法性，而在于当合法性对政治便利构成约束时，谁仍然选择尊重它。

问题的核心，体现出一种熟悉的模式：巫统内部派系试图在一个强调纪律的联盟架构中重新调整影响力。州务大臣的地位，从宪法角度出发，并在森美兰制度中获得强化，原则上应免受周期性派系压力的干扰。然而，当前发展却显示并非如此。正在发生的，并非法律真空，而是将政治竞争叠加在一个原本旨在防止不稳定的制度之上。

因此，“谁”并不模糊。这涉及巫统内部的竞争派系、扎希哈米迪阵营的领导考量、安华依布拉欣政府整体的稳定导向，以及最高元首在四大酋长协商下所行使的制度权威。“什么”同样清晰：这是一种试图以或明或暗的方式影响政治结果的行为，其本质是在测试宪政规范的边界。

时间点同样具有启示意义。这种摩擦出现在选举前的政治环境中，各方正重新定位、巩固影响力，并测试制度极限。这类时刻往往揭示，治理框架究竟是约束政治行为的护栏，还是仅具形式意义的结构。森美兰的制度设计——结合宪法与习俗权威——本应发挥前者的功能。如今，政治行为者是否尊重这一设计，正受到检验。

从治理角度看，州务大臣的合法性并非源自派系背书，而是源自宪政程序。最高元首与四大酋长的参与，为制度提供了一层本应足以缓冲政治波动的监督机制。当派系试图重新诠释或挑战这一结构时，问题已不再是政治分歧，而是制度纪律本身。

在这一点上，安华依布拉欣与扎希哈米迪之间的差异，具有分析意义。根据可观察的政策立场，安华依布拉欣更倾向于制度连续性与联盟稳定。昌明框架依赖可预测性，无法承受由内部派系调整所引发的反复波动。相较之下，扎希哈米迪必须面对巫统内部压力，而这些压力往往将党内整合置于联盟平衡之上。这种张力未必是直接对抗，但却是结构性存在：一方在管理国家联盟，另一方在管理内部仍存分歧的政党。

国盟的立场，则为局势增添另一层复杂性。其定位似乎较少基于宪政一致性，而更多依赖政治机会。当治理框架受到尊重时，反对党应以政策替代方案作为批评重点；当同一框架被选择性挑战时，相关叙事便更接近策略性操作。这种不一致性难以忽视：制度合法性在有利时被维护，在不利时则受到质疑。

因此，这场冲突的“如何发生”，与其“为何发生”同样重要。政治行为者并未公开拆解制度结构，而是在测试其弹性。他们通过叙事建构、选择性诠释宪政规范，以及放大派系不满来实现这一点。这是一种常见策略，但未必具有可持续性。一旦制度被视为可协商对象，其稳定功能便会削弱。

从经济角度看，其影响并非抽象。治理公信力直接影响投资者信心，尤其是在森美兰这样一个政治稳定与发展规划高度关联的州属。投资者更关注制度可预测性，而非单纯的政治竞争。当治理表现被视为取决于派系动态时，风险溢价将随之上升。

更广泛的启示其实相当直接。宪政体系并非自我执行，它依赖政治行为者对法律精神与条文的共同尊重。森美兰融合习俗与宪法权威的制度，本身具备稳固结构。当前紧张局势，并非制度失败，而是制度内政治纪律的考验。

展望未来，数项务实步骤至关重要。首先，各方必须重申最高元首与四大酋长在州体制中的最终仲裁角色。其次，巫统领导层需通过制度化机制解决内部派系问题，而非将其外溢为治理争议。第三，昌明政府必须维持一致立场，将制度连续性置于短期政治妥协之上。最后，反对阵营若要被视为具备替代能力，其批评亦须建立在宪政一致性之上。

森美兰的局势，最终反映出一个更广泛的国家现实：政治公信力，已不再由主张决定，而是由对制度秩序的遵守来衡量。稳定并非口头宣示，而是通过纪律体现。那些将宪政框架视为可灵活操作工具者，最终可能发现，无论是市场、选民还是制度本身，所展现的容忍度远低于预期。

𝙴𝚗𝚐𝚕𝚒𝚜𝚑 𝚅𝚎𝚛𝚜𝚒𝚘𝚗 𝙲𝚘𝚖𝚖𝚎𝚗𝚝𝚊𝚛𝚢

Negeri Sembilan’s current political-institutional conflict is less a crisis of numbers than a test of constitutional maturity. The state’s unique adat-based governance framework, anchored by the Tuanku Yang di-Pertuan Besar and the Undang Yang Empat, is now intersecting with factional manoeuvring within UMNO, recalibration within the MADANI Unity Government, and opportunistic repositioning by Perikatan Nasional. The central question is not who claims legitimacy, but who respects it when it constrains political convenience.

At the core of the issue lies a familiar pattern: internal UMNO factions attempting to recalibrate influence within a coalition structure that demands discipline. The Menteri Besar’s position, constitutionally grounded and reinforced through the Negeri Sembilan system, should in principle be insulated from episodic factional pressure. Yet developments suggest otherwise. What is unfolding is not a legal vacuum, but a political contest layered onto a system that was designed precisely to prevent instability.

The “who” is therefore not ambiguous. It involves competing UMNO factions, leadership calculations within Zahid Hamidi’s camp, the broader stabilising intent of Anwar Ibrahim’s administration, and the institutional authority of the Tuanku Yang di-Pertuan Besar acting in consultation with the Undang Yang Empat. The “what” is equally clear: an attempt, subtle or otherwise, to influence political outcomes in ways that test the boundaries of constitutional propriety.

Timing, as always, is instructive. The friction emerges in a pre-election environment where political actors are recalibrating positions, consolidating influence, and testing institutional limits. Such moments often reveal whether governance frameworks function as guardrails or mere formalities. Negeri Sembilan’s system, with its layered constitutional and customary authority, is designed to act as the former. Whether political actors respect that design is now under scrutiny.

From a governance perspective, the Menteri Besar’s legitimacy is not derived from factional endorsement but from constitutional process. The involvement of the Tuanku Yang di-Pertuan Besar and the Undang Yang Empat introduces a level of institutional oversight that should, in theory, neutralise political volatility. When factions attempt to reinterpret or challenge that structure, the issue is no longer political disagreement but institutional discipline.

This is where the divergence between Anwar Ibrahim and Zahid Hamidi becomes analytically significant. Anwar Ibrahim’s position, based on observable policy posture, reflects a preference for institutional continuity and coalition stability. The MADANI framework depends on predictability; it cannot afford episodic disruptions driven by internal factional recalibration. Zahid Hamidi, on the other hand, must navigate internal UMNO pressures that often prioritise party consolidation over coalition equilibrium. The tension is not necessarily confrontational, but it is structurally embedded. One side is managing a national coalition; the other is managing a party with unresolved internal alignments.

Perikatan Nasional’s stance adds another layer of complexity. Its positioning appears less anchored in constitutional consistency and more in political opportunity. When governance frameworks are respected, opposition critique should focus on policy alternatives. When the same frameworks are selectively challenged, the narrative begins to resemble tactical opportunism. The inconsistency is difficult to ignore: institutional legitimacy is defended when advantageous and questioned when inconvenient.

The “how” of this conflict is therefore as important as the “why.” Political actors are not openly dismantling institutional structures; they are testing their elasticity. This is done through narrative framing, selective interpretation of constitutional norms, and the amplification of factional grievances. It is a familiar strategy, though not necessarily a sustainable one. Institutions, once perceived as negotiable, lose their stabilising function.

From an economic perspective, the implications are not abstract. Governance credibility directly influences investor confidence, particularly in a state like Negeri Sembilan where political stability is intertwined with development planning. Investors are less concerned with political competition than with institutional predictability. When governance appears contingent on factional dynamics, risk premia adjust accordingly.

The broader lesson is straightforward. Constitutional systems are not self-enforcing; they rely on political actors to respect both the letter and the spirit of the law. Negeri Sembilan’s framework, with its integration of adat and constitutional authority, provides a robust structure. The current tension is therefore not a failure of the system, but a test of political discipline within it.

Moving forward, several practical steps are necessary. First, all parties must reaffirm the constitutional role of the Tuanku Yang di-Pertuan Besar and the Undang Yang Empat as final arbiters within the state framework. Second, UMNO leadership must address internal factionalism through structured mechanisms rather than externalising it into governance disputes. Third, the MADANI administration must maintain a consistent stance that prioritises institutional continuity over short-term political accommodation. Finally, opposition actors must align critique with constitutional consistency if they are to be regarded as credible alternatives.

Negeri Sembilan’s situation ultimately illustrates a broader national truth: political credibility is no longer determined by assertion, but by adherence to institutional order. Stability is not merely declared; it is demonstrated through discipline. Those who treat constitutional frameworks as flexible instruments may find that markets, voters, and institutions themselves are far less accommodating.

🗓️ April 28, 2026 | 森美兰权力与原则的考验：当宪政秩序遇上政治野心
𝙲𝚑𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚜𝚎 𝚅𝚎𝚛𝚜𝚒𝚘𝚗 𝙲𝚘𝚖𝚖𝚎𝚗𝚝𝚊𝚛𝚢

森美兰当前的政治与制度冲突，与其说是数字上的危机，不如说是一场宪政成熟度的考验。该州以“习俗法”（adat）为基础的独特治理体系，由最高元首端姑严端大臣（Tuanku Yang di-Pertuan Besar）与四大酋长（Undang Yang Empat）为核心，如今正与巫统内部派系运作、昌明团结政府（MADANI）的政策再校准，以及国盟（Perikatan Nasional）的策略性调整交织在一起。关键问题不在于谁声称拥有合法性，而在于当合法性对政治便利构成约束时，谁仍然选择尊重它。

问题的核心，体现出一种熟悉的模式：巫统内部派系试图在一个强调纪律的联盟架构中重新调整影响力。州务大臣的地位，从宪法角度出发，并在森美兰制度中获得强化，原则上应免受周期性派系压力的干扰。然而，当前发展却显示并非如此。正在发生的，并非法律真空，而是将政治竞争叠加在一个原本旨在防止不稳定的制度之上。

因此，“谁”并不模糊。这涉及巫统内部的竞争派系、扎希哈米迪阵营的领导考量、安华依布拉欣政府整体的稳定导向，以及最高元首在四大酋长协商下所行使的制度权威。“什么”同样清晰：这是一种试图以或明或暗的方式影响政治结果的行为，其本质是在测试宪政规范的边界。

时间点同样具有启示意义。这种摩擦出现在选举前的政治环境中，各方正重新定位、巩固影响力，并测试制度极限。这类时刻往往揭示，治理框架究竟是约束政治行为的护栏，还是仅具形式意义的结构。森美兰的制度设计——结合宪法与习俗权威——本应发挥前者的功能。如今，政治行为者是否尊重这一设计，正受到检验。

从治理角度看，州务大臣的合法性并非源自派系背书，而是源自宪政程序。最高元首与四大酋长的参与，为制度提供了一层本应足以缓冲政治波动的监督机制。当派系试图重新诠释或挑战这一结构时，问题已不再是政治分歧，而是制度纪律本身。

在这一点上，安华依布拉欣与扎希哈米迪之间的差异，具有分析意义。根据可观察的政策立场，安华依布拉欣更倾向于制度连续性与联盟稳定。昌明框架依赖可预测性，无法承受由内部派系调整所引发的反复波动。相较之下，扎希哈米迪必须面对巫统内部压力，而这些压力往往将党内整合置于联盟平衡之上。这种张力未必是直接对抗，但却是结构性存在：一方在管理国家联盟，另一方在管理内部仍存分歧的政党。

国盟的立场，则为局势增添另一层复杂性。其定位似乎较少基于宪政一致性，而更多依赖政治机会。当治理框架受到尊重时，反对党应以政策替代方案作为批评重点；当同一框架被选择性挑战时，相关叙事便更接近策略性操作。这种不一致性难以忽视：制度合法性在有利时被维护，在不利时则受到质疑。

因此，这场冲突的“如何发生”，与其“为何发生”同样重要。政治行为者并未公开拆解制度结构，而是在测试其弹性。他们通过叙事建构、选择性诠释宪政规范，以及放大派系不满来实现这一点。这是一种常见策略，但未必具有可持续性。一旦制度被视为可协商对象，其稳定功能便会削弱。

从经济角度看，其影响并非抽象。治理公信力直接影响投资者信心，尤其是在森美兰这样一个政治稳定与发展规划高度关联的州属。投资者更关注制度可预测性，而非单纯的政治竞争。当治理表现被视为取决于派系动态时，风险溢价将随之上升。

更广泛的启示其实相当直接。宪政体系并非自我执行，它依赖政治行为者对法律精神与条文的共同尊重。森美兰融合习俗与宪法权威的制度，本身具备稳固结构。当前紧张局势，并非制度失败，而是制度内政治纪律的考验。

展望未来，数项务实步骤至关重要。首先，各方必须重申最高元首与四大酋长在州体制中的最终仲裁角色。其次，巫统领导层需通过制度化机制解决内部派系问题，而非将其外溢为治理争议。第三，昌明政府必须维持一致立场，将制度连续性置于短期政治妥协之上。最后，反对阵营若要被视为具备替代能力，其批评亦须建立在宪政一致性之上。

森美兰的局势，最终反映出一个更广泛的国家现实：政治公信力，已不再由主张决定，而是由对制度秩序的遵守来衡量。稳定并非口头宣示，而是通过纪律体现。那些将宪政框架视为可灵活操作工具者，最终可能发现，无论是市场、选民还是制度本身，所展现的容忍度远低于预期。

🗓️ April 28, 2026 | Negeri Sembilan’s Test Of Power And Principle: When Constitutional Order Meets Political Ambition 
𝙴𝚗𝚐𝚕𝚒𝚜𝚑 𝚅𝚎𝚛𝚜𝚒𝚘𝚗 𝙲𝚘𝚖𝚖𝚎𝚗𝚝𝚊𝚛𝚢

Negeri Sembilan’s current political-institutional conflict is less a crisis of numbers than a test of constitutional maturity. The state’s unique adat-based governance framework, anchored by the Tuanku Yang di-Pertuan Besar and the Undang Yang Empat, is now intersecting with factional manoeuvring within UMNO, recalibration within the MADANI Unity Government, and opportunistic repositioning by Perikatan Nasional. The central question is not who claims legitimacy, but who respects it when it constrains political convenience.

At the core of the issue lies a familiar pattern: internal UMNO factions attempting to recalibrate influence within a coalition structure that demands discipline. The Menteri Besar’s position, constitutionally grounded and reinforced through the Negeri Sembilan system, should in principle be insulated from episodic factional pressure. Yet developments suggest otherwise. What is unfolding is not a legal vacuum, but a political contest layered onto a system that was designed precisely to prevent instability.

The “who” is therefore not ambiguous. It involves competing UMNO factions, leadership calculations within Zahid Hamidi’s camp, the broader stabilising intent of Anwar Ibrahim’s administration, and the institutional authority of the Tuanku Yang di-Pertuan Besar acting in consultation with the Undang Yang Empat. The “what” is equally clear: an attempt, subtle or otherwise, to influence political outcomes in ways that test the boundaries of constitutional propriety.

Timing, as always, is instructive. The friction emerges in a pre-election environment where political actors are recalibrating positions, consolidating influence, and testing institutional limits. Such moments often reveal whether governance frameworks function as guardrails or mere formalities. Negeri Sembilan’s system, with its layered constitutional and customary authority, is designed to act as the former. Whether political actors respect that design is now under scrutiny.

From a governance perspective, the Menteri Besar’s legitimacy is not derived from factional endorsement but from constitutional process. The involvement of the Tuanku Yang di-Pertuan Besar and the Undang Yang Empat introduces a level of institutional oversight that should, in theory, neutralise political volatility. When factions attempt to reinterpret or challenge that structure, the issue is no longer political disagreement but institutional discipline.

This is where the divergence between Anwar Ibrahim and Zahid Hamidi becomes analytically significant. Anwar Ibrahim’s position, based on observable policy posture, reflects a preference for institutional continuity and coalition stability. The MADANI framework depends on predictability; it cannot afford episodic disruptions driven by internal factional recalibration. Zahid Hamidi, on the other hand, must navigate internal UMNO pressures that often prioritise party consolidation over coalition equilibrium. The tension is not necessarily confrontational, but it is structurally embedded. One side is managing a national coalition; the other is managing a party with unresolved internal alignments.

Perikatan Nasional’s stance adds another layer of complexity. Its positioning appears less anchored in constitutional consistency and more in political opportunity. When governance frameworks are respected, opposition critique should focus on policy alternatives. When the same frameworks are selectively challenged, the narrative begins to resemble tactical opportunism. The inconsistency is difficult to ignore: institutional legitimacy is defended when advantageous and questioned when inconvenient.

The “how” of this conflict is therefore as important as the “why.” Political actors are not openly dismantling institutional structures; they are testing their elasticity. This is done through narrative framing, selective interpretation of constitutional norms, and the amplification of factional grievances. It is a familiar strategy, though not necessarily a sustainable one. Institutions, once perceived as negotiable, lose their stabilising function.

From an economic perspective, the implications are not abstract. Governance credibility directly influences investor confidence, particularly in a state like Negeri Sembilan where political stability is intertwined with development planning. Investors are less concerned with political competition than with institutional predictability. When governance appears contingent on factional dynamics, risk premia adjust accordingly.

The broader lesson is straightforward. Constitutional systems are not self-enforcing; they rely on political actors to respect both the letter and the spirit of the law. Negeri Sembilan’s framework, with its integration of adat and constitutional authority, provides a robust structure. The current tension is therefore not a failure of the system, but a test of political discipline within it.

Moving forward, several practical steps are necessary. First, all parties must reaffirm the constitutional role of the Tuanku Yang di-Pertuan Besar and the Undang Yang Empat as final arbiters within the state framework. Second, UMNO leadership must address internal factionalism through structured mechanisms rather than externalising it into governance disputes. Third, the MADANI administration must maintain a consistent stance that prioritises institutional continuity over short-term political accommodation. Finally, opposition actors must align critique with constitutional consistency if they are to be regarded as credible alternatives.

Negeri Sembilan’s situation ultimately illustrates a broader national truth: political credibility is no longer determined by assertion, but by adherence to institutional order. Stability is not merely declared; it is demonstrated through discipline. Those who treat constitutional frameworks as flexible instruments may find that markets, voters, and institutions themselves are far less accommodating.

𝙲𝚑𝚒𝚗𝚎𝚜𝚎 𝚅𝚎𝚛𝚜𝚒𝚘𝚗 𝙲𝚘𝚖𝚖𝚎𝚗𝚝𝚊𝚛𝚢

森美兰当前的政治与制度冲突，与其说是数字上的危机，不如说是一场宪政成熟度的考验。该州以“习俗法”（adat）为基础的独特治理体系，由最高元首端姑严端大臣（Tuanku Yang di-Pertuan Besar）与四大酋长（Undang Yang Empat）为核心，如今正与巫统内部派系运作、昌明团结政府（MADANI）的政策再校准，以及国盟（Perikatan Nasional）的策略性调整交织在一起。关键问题不在于谁声称拥有合法性，而在于当合法性对政治便利构成约束时，谁仍然选择尊重它。

问题的核心，体现出一种熟悉的模式：巫统内部派系试图在一个强调纪律的联盟架构中重新调整影响力。州务大臣的地位，从宪法角度出发，并在森美兰制度中获得强化，原则上应免受周期性派系压力的干扰。然而，当前发展却显示并非如此。正在发生的，并非法律真空，而是将政治竞争叠加在一个原本旨在防止不稳定的制度之上。

因此，“谁”并不模糊。这涉及巫统内部的竞争派系、扎希哈米迪阵营的领导考量、安华依布拉欣政府整体的稳定导向，以及最高元首在四大酋长协商下所行使的制度权威。“什么”同样清晰：这是一种试图以或明或暗的方式影响政治结果的行为，其本质是在测试宪政规范的边界。

时间点同样具有启示意义。这种摩擦出现在选举前的政治环境中，各方正重新定位、巩固影响力，并测试制度极限。这类时刻往往揭示，治理框架究竟是约束政治行为的护栏，还是仅具形式意义的结构。森美兰的制度设计——结合宪法与习俗权威——本应发挥前者的功能。如今，政治行为者是否尊重这一设计，正受到检验。

从治理角度看，州务大臣的合法性并非源自派系背书，而是源自宪政程序。最高元首与四大酋长的参与，为制度提供了一层本应足以缓冲政治波动的监督机制。当派系试图重新诠释或挑战这一结构时，问题已不再是政治分歧，而是制度纪律本身。

在这一点上，安华依布拉欣与扎希哈米迪之间的差异，具有分析意义。根据可观察的政策立场，安华依布拉欣更倾向于制度连续性与联盟稳定。昌明框架依赖可预测性，无法承受由内部派系调整所引发的反复波动。相较之下，扎希哈米迪必须面对巫统内部压力，而这些压力往往将党内整合置于联盟平衡之上。这种张力未必是直接对抗，但却是结构性存在：一方在管理国家联盟，另一方在管理内部仍存分歧的政党。

国盟的立场，则为局势增添另一层复杂性。其定位似乎较少基于宪政一致性，而更多依赖政治机会。当治理框架受到尊重时，反对党应以政策替代方案作为批评重点；当同一框架被选择性挑战时，相关叙事便更接近策略性操作。这种不一致性难以忽视：制度合法性在有利时被维护，在不利时则受到质疑。

因此，这场冲突的“如何发生”，与其“为何发生”同样重要。政治行为者并未公开拆解制度结构，而是在测试其弹性。他们通过叙事建构、选择性诠释宪政规范，以及放大派系不满来实现这一点。这是一种常见策略，但未必具有可持续性。一旦制度被视为可协商对象，其稳定功能便会削弱。

从经济角度看，其影响并非抽象。治理公信力直接影响投资者信心，尤其是在森美兰这样一个政治稳定与发展规划高度关联的州属。投资者更关注制度可预测性，而非单纯的政治竞争。当治理表现被视为取决于派系动态时，风险溢价将随之上升。

更广泛的启示其实相当直接。宪政体系并非自我执行，它依赖政治行为者对法律精神与条文的共同尊重。森美兰融合习俗与宪法权威的制度，本身具备稳固结构。当前紧张局势，并非制度失败，而是制度内政治纪律的考验。

展望未来，数项务实步骤至关重要。首先，各方必须重申最高元首与四大酋长在州体制中的最终仲裁角色。其次，巫统领导层需通过制度化机制解决内部派系问题，而非将其外溢为治理争议。第三，昌明政府必须维持一致立场，将制度连续性置于短期政治妥协之上。最后，反对阵营若要被视为具备替代能力，其批评亦须建立在宪政一致性之上。

森美兰的局势，最终反映出一个更广泛的国家现实：政治公信力，已不再由主张决定，而是由对制度秩序的遵守来衡量。稳定并非口头宣示，而是通过纪律体现。那些将宪政框架视为可灵活操作工具者，最终可能发现，无论是市场、选民还是制度本身，所展现的容忍度远低于预期。

🗓️ April 28, 2026 | Negeri Sembilan’s Test Of Power And Principle: When Constitutional Order Meets Political Ambition 
𝙴𝚗𝚐𝚕𝚒𝚜𝚑 𝚅𝚎𝚛𝚜𝚒𝚘𝚗 𝙲𝚘𝚖𝚖𝚎𝚗𝚝𝚊𝚛𝚢

Negeri Sembilan’s current political-institutional conflict is less a crisis of numbers than a test of constitutional maturity. The state’s unique adat-based governance framework, anchored by the Tuanku Yang di-Pertuan Besar and the Undang Yang Empat, is now intersecting with factional manoeuvring within UMNO, recalibration within the MADANI Unity Government, and opportunistic repositioning by Perikatan Nasional. The central question is not who claims legitimacy, but who respects it when it constrains political convenience.

At the core of the issue lies a familiar pattern: internal UMNO factions attempting to recalibrate influence within a coalition structure that demands discipline. The Menteri Besar’s position, constitutionally grounded and reinforced through the Negeri Sembilan system, should in principle be insulated from episodic factional pressure. Yet developments suggest otherwise. What is unfolding is not a legal vacuum, but a political contest layered onto a system that was designed precisely to prevent instability.

The “who” is therefore not ambiguous. It involves competing UMNO factions, leadership calculations within Zahid Hamidi’s camp, the broader stabilising intent of Anwar Ibrahim’s administration, and the institutional authority of the Tuanku Yang di-Pertuan Besar acting in consultation with the Undang Yang Empat. The “what” is equally clear: an attempt, subtle or otherwise, to influence political outcomes in ways that test the boundaries of constitutional propriety.

Timing, as always, is instructive. The friction emerges in a pre-election environment where political actors are recalibrating positions, consolidating influence, and testing institutional limits. Such moments often reveal whether governance frameworks function as guardrails or mere formalities. Negeri Sembilan’s system, with its layered constitutional and customary authority, is designed to act as the former. Whether political actors respect that design is now under scrutiny.

From a governance perspective, the Menteri Besar’s legitimacy is not derived from factional endorsement but from constitutional process. The involvement of the Tuanku Yang di-Pertuan Besar and the Undang Yang Empat introduces a level of institutional oversight that should, in theory, neutralise political volatility. When factions attempt to reinterpret or challenge that structure, the issue is no longer political disagreement but institutional discipline.

This is where the divergence between Anwar Ibrahim and Zahid Hamidi becomes analytically significant. Anwar Ibrahim’s position, based on observable policy posture, reflects a preference for institutional continuity and coalition stability. The MADANI framework depends on predictability; it cannot afford episodic disruptions driven by internal factional recalibration. Zahid Hamidi, on the other hand, must navigate internal UMNO pressures that often prioritise party consolidation over coalition equilibrium. The tension is not necessarily confrontational, but it is structurally embedded. One side is managing a national coalition; the other is managing a party with unresolved internal alignments.

Perikatan Nasional’s stance adds another layer of complexity. Its positioning appears less anchored in constitutional consistency and more in political opportunity. When governance frameworks are respected, opposition critique should focus on policy alternatives. When the same frameworks are selectively challenged, the narrative begins to resemble tactical opportunism. The inconsistency is difficult to ignore: institutional legitimacy is defended when advantageous and questioned when inconvenient.

The “how” of this conflict is therefore as important as the “why.” Political actors are not openly dismantling institutional structures; they are testing their elasticity. This is done through narrative framing, selective interpretation of constitutional norms, and the amplification of factional grievances. It is a familiar strategy, though not necessarily a sustainable one. Institutions, once perceived as negotiable, lose their stabilising function.

From an economic perspective, the implications are not abstract. Governance credibility directly influences investor confidence, particularly in a state like Negeri Sembilan where political stability is intertwined with development planning. Investors are less concerned with political competition than with institutional predictability. When governance appears contingent on factional dynamics, risk premia adjust accordingly.

The broader lesson is straightforward. Constitutional systems are not self-enforcing; they rely on political actors to respect both the letter and the spirit of the law. Negeri Sembilan’s framework, with its integration of adat and constitutional authority, provides a robust structure. The current tension is therefore not a failure of the system, but a test of political discipline within it.

Moving forward, several practical steps are necessary. First, all parties must reaffirm the constitutional role of the Tuanku Yang di-Pertuan Besar and the Undang Yang Empat as final arbiters within the state framework. Second, UMNO leadership must address internal factionalism through structured mechanisms rather than externalising it into governance disputes. Third, the MADANI administration must maintain a consistent stance that prioritises institutional continuity over short-term political accommodation. Finally, opposition actors must align critique with constitutional consistency if they are to be regarded as credible alternatives.

Negeri Sembilan’s situation ultimately illustrates a broader national truth: political credibility is no longer determined by assertion, but by adherence to institutional order. Stability is not merely declared; it is demonstrated through discipline. Those who treat constitutional frameworks as flexible instruments may find that markets, voters, and institutions themselves are far less accommodating.

UMNO and Barisan Nasional (BN) have officially withdrawn their support for Negeri Sembilan Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Aminuddin Harun, triggering a political crisis in the state

The 14 UMNO assemblymen reached a unanimous decision on 27 April, at Wisma UMNO. UMNO is a component party of the BN coalition. In a press conference, Negeri Sembilan UMNO Liaison Committee chairman Datuk Seri Jalaluddin Alias said all 14 assemblymen were withdrawing their support for the state government. According to the New Straits Times, they cited a loss in confidence in the menteri besar over his handling of a royal constitutional dispute involving the Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir.Negeri Sembilan is unique among Malaysian states for having an elected, rather than strictly hereditary, monarchy rooted in the Adat Perpatih matrilineal systemUnlike other Malay states where the eldest son typically becomes the Sultan, in Negeri Sembilan, the Yang di-Pertuan Besar (or Yamtuan Besar) is chosen by the four ruling chiefs, known as the Undang Yang Empat.

The Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir was chosen as the state's monarch following the Adat Perpatih customs and laws.

The political crisis began on 19 April when four Negeri Sembilan Undangs, led by former Undang of Sungei Ujong Datuk Mubarak Dohak, declared the removal of the state's monarch, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, citing alleged "misconduct"

According to The Star, Mubarak, together with Undang Jelebu Datuk Maarof Mat Rashad, Undang Johol Datuk Muhammed Abdullah, and Undang Rembau Datuk Abdul Rahim Yasin, held a meeting and reached an agreement to remove Tuanku Muhriz as the state's monarch.They did not elaborate or specify the alleged misconduct. In the same declaration, the Undangs named Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja'afar (the Tunku Panglima Besar) as the 12th Yang di-Pertuan Besar.Tunku Nadzaruddin is the son of Tuanku Ja'afar, who served as the Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan from 1967 to 2008.

Negeri Sembilan Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Aminuddin Harun (centre) flanked by DAP secretary-general Anthony Loke (left) and Negeri Sembilan Amanah chairman Datuk MK Ibrahim Abd Rahman.

The following day, 20 April, Aminuddin dismissed Mubarak's declaration as illegal, saying he lacked the authority to make such a move

In a statement, Aminuddin cited Articles 10 to 13 of the Laws of the Constitution of Negri Sembilan 1959, explaining that Mubarak no longer held the authority as he was removed as the Undang on 13 May 2025.Mubarak was allegedly removed due to 33 customary offences, which were not specified by Aminuddin.On 17 April, the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang (DKU) — the constitutional body that manages traditional royal affairs for the Negeri Sembilan monarchy — sat and advised that his dismissal be accepted.Under the advice of the Telaga Undang and Waris Klana Hulu Sg Ujong, Mubarak was removed as Undang.The Telaga Undang also confirmed that Mubarak had been removed and described his actions as an act of treason.

Despite the loss of UMNO support, Aminuddin confirmed he would continue his duties as menteri besar as normal and lead a 'minority government' without having to dissolve the Negeri Sembilan state assembly

According to Malaysiakini, this decision comes following instructions he received from Tuanku Muhriz after briefing him on the situation on 27 April. The Democratic Action Party (DAP), which is part of the Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition alongside Aminuddin's Parti Keadilan Rakyat (PKR), has also stood by the current menteri besar. Secretary-General Anthony Loke confirmed that all 11 DAP assemblymen still support Aminuddin's leadership.Negeri Sembilan has 36 state seats. Following the state election in 2023, BN formed the state government together with PH after winning 31 seats.With the BN assemblymen leaving the state government, the current seat composition in the state is as follows:

Pakatan Harapan (PH): 17

Barisan Nasional (BH): 14

Perikatan Nasional (PN): 5

Meanwhile, Harian Metro reported that the five assemblymen from PN are reportedly ready to cooperate with UMNO to ensure administrative continuity in the state.

UMNO president Datuk Seri Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said the move by the BN state assemblymen to leave the Negeri Sembilan PH coalition was made at the state level

According to the New Straits Times, he said the matter will be discussed at the UMNO Supreme Council and UMNO Political Bureau meetings.He added that UMNO and BN will not interfere in state governance and customary laws, as the crisis will be resolved politically.Meanwhile, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said that a state election is unlikely as it depends on the decision made by Tuanku Muhriz.

A political expert said there are only two ways the Negeri Sembilan political crisis could unfold

Speaking to Harian Metro, political analyst Mohammad Tawfik Yaakub from Universiti Malaya said the first is the dissolution of the state assembly for a fresh state election.The second option is the formation of a new political partnership.However, he noted that a formal alliance between UMNO and PN remains difficult at this stage.

Two Wrongs, One Reality: A  Rebuttal to the “September 16” Moral Lecture

(As rebuttal to this : https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1B66NB9TRq/) 

Yeo Bee Yin’s line :“two wrongs don’t make a right” sounds tidy, principled, and eminently tweetable. The problem is that Malaysian politics is not a moral philosophy seminar; it’s a system built on contingencies, coalitions, and when push comes to shove numbers. Invoking September 16 as a tired relic misses the point Khairy Jamaluddin was making. He wasn’t pleading precedent as justification. He was reminding everyone that Malaysia’s political playbook has long included mid-stream realignments. Calling that history “tired” doesn’t make it untrue; it just makes it inconvenient.

1) The “Unity Government” isn’t a marriage; it’s a ceasefire

Let’s start with the big premise. The so-called unity government was never a pre-election covenant. It was a post-election arrangement born of arithmetic and necessity. No manifesto promised it. No voter explicitly endorsed it as a package. It was, to be blunt, a circumstantial coalition constructed to prevent deadlock, not to sanctify permanence.

If something is circumstantially created, it can be circumstantially undone. That’s not sabotage; that’s symmetry. Treating a post-election patchwork as if it were a sacred, pre-election mandate is a category error. Stability matters, yes but stability built on denial of political reality tends to be… temporary.

2) Negeri Sembilan isn’t “destabilization”; it’s a collision of systems

Framing the Negeri Sembilan episode as pure “destabilization” flattens a far more complex picture. This is not just about numbers in a legislative chamber. It’s about a state where constitutional authority intersects with Adat Perpatih, where the Yang di-Pertuan Besar and the Undang Yang Empat are not decorative but foundational.

When a Menteri Besar is seen to be taking sides in a dispute involving these institutions, the issue ceases to be routine politics. It becomes a question of institutional propriety. In such a context, insisting on business-as-usual parliamentary etiquette while ignoring adat sensitivities is not moral clarity; it’s selective blindness.

So no, this isn’t simply a “topple the government” play. It’s a stress test of whether political actors understand the ecosystem they operate in. If anything looks destabilizing, it is the mixing of partisan instincts with institutions that were historically kept above the fray.

3) KJ isn’t endorsing chaos; he’s describing the rulebook

Khairy Jamaluddin’s commentary did not say, “Do it because someone did it in 2008.” He said, in effect, “This is how the system has worked before and still can.” That’s a descriptive claim, not a moral endorsement.

Citing Zambry v Nizar isn’t a call to arms; it’s a reminder that loss of confidence can be established beyond a formal vote. You may dislike the doctrine. You may wish it didn’t exist. But it does. Shooting the messenger for pointing it out is an odd way to argue constitutional purity.

4) Why the defensiveness? Follow the geography

The sharper question is not why KJ said what he said but why it stings. Negeri Sembilan is not abstract terrain. It is home ground to a senior DAP figure with deep local roots and influence. When politics, adat, and local networks intersect, sensitivities rise.

Defensiveness, then, is not surprising. But let’s not pretend it’s purely about high principle. There is a local dimension here one that makes any perceived shift in power or narrative feel more immediate, more personal, and yes, more uncomfortable.

5) UMNO’s move: late opportunism or delayed response?

If opportunism were the goal, the window opened much earlier. Post-election, a BN–PN configuration was numerically plausible. It didn’t happen. For nearly three years, the arrangement held. Only when the institutional dispute escalated did support get pulled.

You can disagree with the timing or the judgment. But calling it a crude “he did it first” move ignores the chronology. Sometimes, what looks like opportunism is simply a threshold being crossed.

6) The generational argument cuts both ways

Invoking young voters as moral arbiters is clever, but selective. Are we telling them politics must ignore precedent? That coalitions formed after elections are sacrosanct? That institutional disputes should be subsumed under party discipline?

If the lesson is that politics should be cleaner, fair enough. But then the standard must be applied consistently across parties, across episodes, across time. Otherwise, it’s not a principle; it’s branding.

7) The uncomfortable truth

Malaysia’s political system allows for mid-term reconfiguration. Negeri Sembilan’s system adds another layer where adat legitimacy matters alongside constitutional mechanics. Pretending either layer doesn’t exist is how crises deepen.

So yes, “two wrongs don’t make a right” sounds right. But in a system like this, the more useful question is: what actually stabilizes the state now? A rigid reading of a circumstantial pact, or a recalibration that acknowledges both numbers and institutions?

Khairy’s answer is unsentimental: understand the system as it is, not as we wish it to be. If that feels uncomfortable, it’s probably because it’s closer to reality than we’d like.

森美兰当前的政治与制度冲突，与其说是数字上的危机，不如说是一场宪政成熟度的考验。该州以“习俗法”（adat）为基础的独特治理体系，由最高元首端姑严端大臣（Tuanku Yang di-Pertuan Besar）与四大酋长（Undang Yang Empat）为核心，如今正与巫统内部派系运作、昌明团结政府（MADANI）的政策再校准，以及国盟（Perikatan Nasional）的策略性调整交织在一起。关键问题不在于谁声称拥有合法性，而在于当合法性对政治便利构成约束时，谁仍然选择尊重它。

问题的核心，体现出一种熟悉的模式：巫统内部派系试图在一个强调纪律的联盟架构中重新调整影响力。州务大臣的地位，从宪法角度出发，并在森美兰制度中获得强化，原则上应免受周期性派系压力的干扰。然而，当前发展却显示并非如此。正在发生的，并非法律真空，而是将政治竞争叠加在一个原本旨在防止不稳定的制度之上。

因此，“谁”并不模糊。这涉及巫统内部的竞争派系、扎希哈米迪阵营的领导考量、安华依布拉欣政府整体的稳定导向，以及最高元首在四大酋长协商下所行使的制度权威。“什么”同样清晰：这是一种试图以或明或暗的方式影响政治结果的行为，其本质是在测试宪政规范的边界。

时间点同样具有启示意义。这种摩擦出现在选举前的政治环境中，各方正重新定位、巩固影响力，并测试制度极限。这类时刻往往揭示，治理框架究竟是约束政治行为的护栏，还是仅具形式意义的结构。森美兰的制度设计——结合宪法与习俗权威——本应发挥前者的功能。如今，政治行为者是否尊重这一设计，正受到检验。

从治理角度看，州务大臣的合法性并非源自派系背书，而是源自宪政程序。最高元首与四大酋长的参与，为制度提供了一层本应足以缓冲政治波动的监督机制。当派系试图重新诠释或挑战这一结构时，问题已不再是政治分歧，而是制度纪律本身。

在这一点上，安华依布拉欣与扎希哈米迪之间的差异，具有分析意义。根据可观察的政策立场，安华依布拉欣更倾向于制度连续性与联盟稳定。昌明框架依赖可预测性，无法承受由内部派系调整所引发的反复波动。相较之下，扎希哈米迪必须面对巫统内部压力，而这些压力往往将党内整合置于联盟平衡之上。这种张力未必是直接对抗，但却是结构性存在：一方在管理国家联盟，另一方在管理内部仍存分歧的政党。

国盟的立场，则为局势增添另一层复杂性。其定位似乎较少基于宪政一致性，而更多依赖政治机会。当治理框架受到尊重时，反对党应以政策替代方案作为批评重点；当同一框架被选择性挑战时，相关叙事便更接近策略性操作。这种不一致性难以忽视：制度合法性在有利时被维护，在不利时则受到质疑。

因此，这场冲突的“如何发生”，与其“为何发生”同样重要。政治行为者并未公开拆解制度结构，而是在测试其弹性。他们通过叙事建构、选择性诠释宪政规范，以及放大派系不满来实现这一点。这是一种常见策略，但未必具有可持续性。一旦制度被视为可协商对象，其稳定功能便会削弱。

从经济角度看，其影响并非抽象。治理公信力直接影响投资者信心，尤其是在森美兰这样一个政治稳定与发展规划高度关联的州属。投资者更关注制度可预测性，而非单纯的政治竞争。当治理表现被视为取决于派系动态时，风险溢价将随之上升。

更广泛的启示其实相当直接。宪政体系并非自我执行，它依赖政治行为者对法律精神与条文的共同尊重。森美兰融合习俗与宪法权威的制度，本身具备稳固结构。当前紧张局势，并非制度失败，而是制度内政治纪律的考验。

展望未来，数项务实步骤至关重要。首先，各方必须重申最高元首与四大酋长在州体制中的最终仲裁角色。其次，巫统领导层需通过制度化机制解决内部派系问题，而非将其外溢为治理争议。第三，昌明政府必须维持一致立场，将制度连续性置于短期政治妥协之上。最后，反对阵营若要被视为具备替代能力，其批评亦须建立在宪政一致性之上。

森美兰的局势，最终反映出一个更广泛的国家现实：政治公信力，已不再由主张决定，而是由对制度秩序的遵守来衡量。稳定并非口头宣示，而是通过纪律体现。那些将宪政框架视为可灵活操作工具者，最终可能发现，无论是市场、选民还是制度本身，所展现的容忍度远低于预期。
